clue.text: For that matter grey can't be made white by indoctrination

definitions.text: For that matter grey can't be made white

explanation.surface: A remark that grey things can never be made white again, tacked onto a word about indoctrination.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half plays on 'grey matter', the brain: it cannot be washed white. The second half is the plain sense, persuasion by relentless indoctrination.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleaning grey matter would literally scrub the brain; the everyday term means forcing beliefs on someone through systematic indoctrination.

clue.text: They're all of a twitter, being a bit under par ?

definitions.text: They're all of a twitter, being a bit under par ?

parts.words: They're all of a twitter, being a bit under par
parts.note: creatures that twitter, and golf holes completed one stroke below the expected score

explanation.surface: Some people are nervous and agitated because they feel slightly unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under par' suggests feeling poorly; in golf it means fewer strokes than standard, and one under is a bird's name. 'All of a twitter' means flustered, but birds twitter.
explanation.definitionFit: Songbirds chirp, and golfers name a hole played in one stroke below the standard after them.

clue.text: A tartan type hat ?

parts.note: a Scot is the kind of person who wears tartan

explanation.surface: Asking about a hat in tartan cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: Ascot, the racecourse, is famous for elaborate hats at Royal Ascot, and the word has named a style of hat.
explanation.definitionFit: An Ascot is also a style of headwear, named after the racecourse where flamboyant millinery is paraded.

clue.text: Always thoughtless? Doesn't matter

explanation.surface: Someone who forgets everything shrugs it off as unimportant.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, 'never' plus 'mind' is never thinking; the phrase is also a shrug meaning the matter is unimportant.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally, at no time having thought in one's head; idiomatically, a dismissive phrase that something is unimportant.

clue.text: Operatic affectations ?

explanation.surface: Wondering whether opera singers are given to putting on pretensions.
explanation.walkthrough: Operatic tunes are songs; putting on 'graces' is giving yourself superior manners.
explanation.definitionFit: Songs sung solo in an opera, and pretentious manners put on to impress, share the word.

clue.text: Whose misleading cases? The answer's fishy

definitions.text: Whose misleading cases? The answer's fishy

parts.words: Whose misleading cases? The answer's fishy
parts.note: A. P. Herbert's 'Misleading Cases' starred the litigant Albert Haddock, whose surname is also a sea fish

explanation.surface: Someone asks who owns some deceptive boxes, and finds the reply suspicious.
explanation.walkthrough: A. P. Herbert's humorous mock law reports, 'Misleading Cases', feature the persistent litigant Albert Haddock; the plural name is also a type of cod-family fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The litigant's surname is a sea fish of the cod family, so the possessive also names fish.

clue.text: In the main a dirty low-down spot

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Somewhere out at sea is a filthy, disreputable place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' picks the letters out of 'maiN A DIRty'. 'The main' is the open sea, which keeps the surface nautical.
explanation.definitionFit: The nadir is the lowest point of anything, the bottom spot.

clue.text: Saint Robert Scot has one town in Ireland:

parts.note: Rab is the Scottish short form of Robert
ane is the Scots word for one

explanation.surface: A Scottish saint named Robert owns a single Irish town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scot' tells you to use Scots forms: Rab for Robert and ane for one. Strabane is a town in County Tyrone, Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Strabane is a market town in County Tyrone on the border of Northern Ireland.

clue.text: Flung about fifty-—what defence?

indicators.note: the word for flung goes round the letter for fifty

parts.note: shied means threw or flung
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Someone throwing something about fifty times asks what protection there is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts L inside SHIED.
explanation.definitionFit: A shield is a piece of armour held up as protection, a means of defence.

clue.text: Gamp better ?

parts.note: a gamp is an old word for an umbrella, after Mrs Gamp in Dickens; one made better has been given a new cover, and a person made better is well again

explanation.surface: A one-line query about an umbrella that has been mended.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Gamp in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit carried a bulky umbrella, so 'gamp' became slang for one. Split it as RE-COVERED for the umbrella; as one word it means restored to health.
explanation.definitionFit: An umbrella given fresh fabric has a new cover, while 'better' in health means restored after illness.

clue.text: Was Mrs. Coster a Miss Hook?

definitions.text: Was Mrs. Coster a Miss Hook?

parts.words: Was Mrs. Coster a Miss Hook
parts.note: a costermonger's wife is 'my old' one of these in the music-hall song, and Miss Hook came from Holland in the Edwardian musical comedy

explanation.surface: A question whether a street trader's wife was once the heroine of a musical.
explanation.walkthrough: A coster (costermonger) was a London street barrow-seller; Albert Chevalier's song 'My Old Dutch' calls his wife that. 'Miss Hook of Holland' was a 1907 musical, so a Miss Hook was a Hollander.
explanation.definitionFit: Cockney slang for a wife and the nationality of Holland's people share the one word.

clue.text: Is sending down under

parts.note: reads like talk of travel to Australia, but means placing a body down under the earth

explanation.surface: Someone is dispatching a traveller to Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down under' suggests Australia; the real sense is a burial, putting someone down beneath the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: To bury a body is to lower it below ground, so the verb for burial fits 'is sending down under'.

clue.text: For the relief of those who didn't make the good time

definitions.text: For the relief of those who didn't make the good time

parts.words: For the relief of those who didn't make the good time
parts.note: sounds like a race where some runners were slow, but describes a local tax levied to relieve paupers; a slow pace is a bad speed

explanation.surface: Comfort for athletes who failed to finish in a good time.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a race; a slow runner's pace is a 'poor rate'. Historically the poor rate was a parish tax in England funding relief of the destitute.
explanation.definitionFit: The old English parish levy paid for poor relief, and a bad pace is a feeble speed.

clue.text: Sally alters the image of the tories

indicators.note: changing the image of something reshapes it, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A girl named Sally changes how the Conservative party is seen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sally' looks like a woman's name but means a sudden charge out by troops; 'alters the image of' rearranges TORIES.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a sudden attack launched from a besieged position, a military raid.

clue.text: Author holds information put up by a turncoat

indicators.note: the novelist's name contains the next piece

parts.note: Charles Reade was a Victorian novelist, author of The Cloister and the Hearth

indicators.note: in a down clue putting something up writes it bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: gen is slang for information

explanation.surface: A writer is holding information posted by a traitor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' turns GEN into NEG, which READE 'holds': RE-NEG-ADE.
explanation.definitionFit: A renegade deserts one cause or side for another, a turncoat.

clue.text: Oblique and hairless horse

parts.note: skew means slanting or oblique
bald means hairless

explanation.surface: A slanting, hairless horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A skewbald is a horse with patches of white and another colour other than black.

clue.text: Querying a goal can bring Hunter woe

indicators.note: the letters can be brought round into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Questioning whether a goal counts could cause a player called Hunter grief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can bring' rearranges HUNTER WOE. The answer is an old word asking 'to what end?', which queries an aim.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic question means 'to what end?', asking about an aim or purpose.

clue.text: They're mean, and ladies may be loth to do so

definitions.text: ladies may be loth to do so

explanation.surface: Some people are stingy, and women may be reluctant to behave the same way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like stingy but is the statistical mean. Split the answer as AVER AGES: women may be loth to state how old they are.
explanation.definitionFit: Statistical means are typical middle values, and to declare one's years is something many women prefer not to do.

clue.text: Collared winger

parts.note: sounds like a footballer caught by the collar, but describes a bird with a neck band

explanation.surface: A wing forward on the football field is grabbed by the collar.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'winger' is a football position; here it is anything with wings, a pigeon whose neck bears a ring of colour.
explanation.definitionFit: This pigeon has a pale band around its neck, so it is a bird wearing a collar.

clue.text: Come along, Sisyphus !

explanation.surface: Someone urges the Greek king Sisyphus to hurry up.
explanation.walkthrough: A showman's call to gather an audience; and Sisyphus was condemned in Hades to push a boulder up a hill forever.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairground barker's cry to an audience, and the endless labour of pushing a stone uphill.

clue.text: League fittings in boots ?

parts.note: the seven-league boots of fairy tale; a boot size reads as a fitting, so the fittings are in that number

explanation.surface: A question about the studs fitted in football boots for a league match.
explanation.walkthrough: In fairy tales seven-league boots cover seven leagues a stride; 'fittings' treats seven as a boot size.
explanation.definitionFit: Boots described by that number of leagues would carry that figure, as a size or fitting.

clue.text: Artful tinker goes round the gallery looking grand

indicators.note: the word for artful is placed around the gallery's name

parts.note: a crafty tinker is a sly one, artful meaning sly
the Tate is the famous London art gallery

explanation.surface: A crafty travelling mender wanders around the art gallery looking magnificent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Artful tinker' reads as a craftsman, but only his slyness counts. The Tate is London's national gallery of British and modern art.
explanation.definitionFit: Stately means dignified and imposing in appearance, so grand-looking.

clue.text: Fire-vessels ?

parts.note: read one way, devices that make fire; read another, flat-bottomed boats that carry cargo

explanation.surface: A one-word query about ships that carry fire.
explanation.walkthrough: Split at the hyphen: things that start a fire, and vessels, the barges that unload ships in harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: A cigarette igniter and a harbour barge share the same name.

clue.text: Trunk addressed to railway sorting office

parts.note: SO is the abbreviation for sorting office

explanation.surface: A trunk with a label sending it to the railway's sorting office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trunk' looks like luggage in the surface; it is the human body without head and limbs.
explanation.definitionFit: The torso is the main body of a person without head or limbs, the trunk.

clue.text: Let Eva twirl in the dance

indicators.note: to twirl is to spin round, so these letters are spun into a new order

explanation.surface: Let Eva spin round on the dance floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twirl' rearranges LET EVA. The veleta is an old-time round dance in waltz time.
explanation.definitionFit: The veleta is a sequence dance in triple time, popular in British ballrooms.

clue.text: Sends out for this paper perhaps

indicators.note: the name of the paper may perhaps be rearranged into another word

parts.note: the clue appeared in The Times newspaper

explanation.surface: Sending something out, maybe for this very newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this paper' is The Times, where the puzzle was printed; 'perhaps' rearranges its name.
explanation.definitionFit: To emit is to give off or discharge, sending outward.

clue.text: The churchwarden is but mortal

explanation.surface: The parish churchwarden is only human after all.
explanation.walkthrough: A churchwarden here is a long-stemmed pipe made of baked earthenware; the Bible calls human flesh this earth.
explanation.definitionFit: A long earthenware tobacco pipe bears the parish officer's name, and humans are dust or earth by biblical metaphor.

clue.text: Inundated Neath

explanation.surface: The Welsh town of Neath has been flooded.
explanation.walkthrough: Neath is a town in South Wales, but here it is short for 'beneath'. A flooded place is below the water.
explanation.definitionFit: Something flooded lies below water, and the poetic 'neath means below.

clue.text: That's dished the girl Anne rounding it in reverse

parts.note: gal is a familiar word for a girl

indicators.note: Anne goes round the next piece, so she is the container
the word it is written backwards

explanation.surface: Anne, a girl serving up a dish, turns it around backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's dished' means 'that is something served as a dish', not 'that's ruined'; the girl Anne really is the container here.
explanation.definitionFit: Galantine is cold meat or poultry boned, set in jelly and served as a dish.

clue.text: Call of those on Council waiting lists? It's a gamble

definitions.text: Call of those on Council waiting lists

explanation.surface: People queuing for council homes call out, and the whole business is a gamble.
explanation.walkthrough: Council housing is local-authority rented housing in Britain, with long waiting lists. The repeated call was the old name for bingo, a gambling game.
explanation.definitionFit: Families wanting a home would cry for one, and the old bingo-caller's cry named the game of chance.
